One `return`, no `if`, no `Count`/`Any`/`Length` in the method. Ok -> 200 is documented: "A 200 status code is returned with the `Product` object when the product does exist. The `Ok` convenience method is invoked as shorthand for `return new OkObjectResult(product);`"

The `Ok` convenience method is invoked as shorthand for `return new OkObjectResult(product);`"

The whole class body at stage-1 (lines 10-29) contains exactly two `db` calls: `db.Products.Select(...).ToListAsync()` and `db.Products.FindAsync(id)`. No `Add`, `AddAsync`, `Update`, `Remove`, `Attach`, `SaveChanges`, `SaveChangesAsync`, `ExecuteUpdate` or `ExecuteDelete` appears anywhere in the file at that tag.

RFC 9110 9.2.1: "Request methods are considered 'safe' if their defined semantics are essentially read-only; i.e., the client does not request, and does not expect, any state change on the origin server as a result of applying a safe method to a target resource." and "the GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE methods are defined to be safe." 9.2.2: "Of the request methods defined by this specification, PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent." Safe implies idempotent, never the reverse, so safe is the stronger promise.

No document pinned in versions.yaml states the collection rule; source_hint names only "REST convention". It follows from RFC 9110 15.5.5 - "The 404 (Not Found) status code indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists" - plus 15.3.1 "The 200 (OK) status code indicates that the request has succeeded": the collection resource exists whatever its row count. But RFC 9110 nowhere distinguishes collection URLs from item URLs.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: collection GET stays `200` - by the convention this API follows, a collection URL names the whole set, and an empty set is still a complete answer about that set; the row count never turns the answer into a `404` (a URL the server has no collection behind at all, like `/api/v1/gadgets`, is a different case: there is nothing there at all, so this rule says nothing about it).

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 15.5.5, verbatim: "The 404 (Not Found) status code indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists. A 404 status code does not indicate whether this lack of representation is temporary or permanent; the 410 (Gone) status code is preferred over 404 if the origin server knows ... that the condition is likely to be permanent." Both halves of the claim are literal in that paragraph.

Prepending: "The route templates you define on the controller are prepended to route templates on the actions", with the parallel sample "The URL path `/products` can match `ProductsApi.ListProducts`". Constraint table: `int` | `{id:int}` | Example Matches "`123456789`, `-123456789`" | "Matches any integer" - negatives match, as the lesson says. Non-integer segment: "If constraints are used for input validation, invalid input results in a `404` Not Found response", i.e. the constrained route does not match; no other route at stage-1 covers `/api/v1/products/<non-integer>`.

issues.text: The collection-GET rule is stated with no condition, as if HTTP required it. RFC 9110 defines 404 only as "did not find a current representation for the target resource" (15.5.5) and never mentions collection URLs; the rule is an API-design convention that follows from the collection resource existing, and claim 6's own source_hint concedes it ("REST resource-naming convention"). Summary line 2 repeats the unconditioned form.

Keep the `/api/v1/gadgets` exception as written.
